title: The 4x4 inverse block-wise on four lanes
body: The f32 Mat4 inverse uses 2x2 blocks M = [A B; C D] packed one per register: det M = |A||D| + |B||C| - tr(A#B D#C), and the blocks of the inverse are adj(|D|A - B D#C), adj(|B|C - D adj(A#B)), adj(|C|B - A adj(D#C)) and adj(|A|D - C A#B), each over det M (# the adjugate). They are polynomial identities, so no block needs to be invertible; A#B and D#C are shared, about 60 lane operations against about 150 scalar ones by cofactors. Measured (bench/geometry, 1,024 independent inverses, best of 101 alternating rounds): 6.4 us against glam's 8.0 (1.25x), where parda's scalar cofactors were 9.6 against 7.3. Accuracy: on 2,000 transforms with projective rows, its worst error is within 16 units of cond(M) * eps and no worse than cofactors (both about the same; the test asserts within 2x), and the native backend matches the portable arithmetic bit for bit. f64 keeps cofactors (no four-lane f64 register in SSE2), 1.06-1.14x glam's DMat4. Rejected: porting glam's GLM-derived factor shuffles (more shuffles, and the block form is derivable and testable on its own).

title: One set of kernels over a Quad trait, backends per instruction set
body: src/geometry/quad.rs writes the kernels (mul_vec4, mul_mat4, inverse) once over Quad: load, store, store_to, splat, add, sub, mul, div, and shuffles whose pattern is a const generic in SSE's shufps encoding. SSE passes the pattern straight to _mm_shuffle_ps; NEON decodes it at compile time (inline const) into a tbl byte table; wasm into i8x16_swizzle tables (two swizzles and an or for two sources); Portable is plain arrays and runs the same kernels on every host, so the arithmetic is tested where a backend can't run. Dispatch: Mat4 checks TypeId of T against f32 and casts (same() in matrix.rs), constant per instance. Not verified in the assembly that the f64 instance carries no branch, but f64 measures 1.4-1.6x glam on Mat4 * Mat4, which leaves no room for one. Rejected: macro_rules per backend (hygiene-dependent, harder to read), and per-backend const generics for lane indices, which stable Rust can't compute from a pattern parameter (generic_const_exprs).

rests_on.of: design:autodyne / Geometry and lanes / small types#intent

title: Summation orders: Mat4 * Vec4 in sequence, Mat4 * Mat4 in pairs, the same bits on every path
body: Measured in bench/geometry (three builds, best of 101 rounds each): summing m * v column after column, as glam does, is 1.00-1.08x glam and gives glam's bits exactly; summing each product's columns in pairs is 1.01-1.07x glam for Mat4 * Mat4, where the sequence measured 0.91-0.92x. The plain-arithmetic paths (f64, targets without a backend) sum in the same orders, so f32 results are bit-identical whichever path runs. Storing the lanes straight into the result (Quad::store_to) instead of through an array took Mat4 * Vec4 from 0.94x to parity and better; loading Vec4<f32> in place as [f32; 4] (repr(C)) from 0.88x to 0.94x. Code placement alone moves the single-value cases by up to ~8% between builds (glam's own Mat4 product measured 3.14 and 3.40 us in two builds of the same harness), so within that they read as parity.

title: compose_world uses Mat4's SIMD product (reversing the prototype's finding)
body: parda's prototype measured its SSE product 17% slower than glam inside compose_world and plain arithmetic 2% faster, because each product went through memory. Here the product loads the columns in place and stores straight into the result, and inside compose_world it measures 0.99-1.01x glam's loop at 10k and 100k nodes, where plain arithmetic measured 0.92-0.95x. So compose_world calls Mat4's own product; the prototype's note stays as what it measured then.

rests_on.of: design:autodyne / Geometry and lanes / small types#intent

title: Aligning Mat4 to 16 bytes bought nothing
body: To close a 0.92x on Mat4 * Mat4 (glam's Mat4 is 16-byte aligned, so SSE can fold its loads into the arithmetic), Mat4 became #[repr(C, align(16))] with aligned loads: 0.91x and 0.96x in two builds, inside the layout noise. Reverted (no layout change without a measured reason). What closed the gap was storing results straight into place. Lesson: when a single-value kernel trails by under 10%, look at loads and stores through temporaries first, and compare across at least two builds before believing a change (code placement moves these cases by ~8%).

title: bytemuck as an optional feature; dev-dependencies off wasm
body: Pod and Zeroable for the vectors and matrices (f32, f64) come with an optional `bytemuck` feature (default-features off, so no_std), as glam does: parda turns it on, nothing else pays for it, and it only adds impls (rust.features-additive). The crate's dev-dependencies (cpal, midir, criterion, hound, rtrb, serde_json) moved under cfg(not(target_family = "wasm")): no lib test uses them, and they don't build for wasm, where CI now runs the geometry tests under wasmtime with simd128.

title: Committable changes bundled with a status change, then split, broke the proposal
body: Proposal 01a119e7 bundled code links, checks and journal entries (all within record trust) with one status change, so the whole batch waited on the user, and tend check failed on unowned files meanwhile. Committing the links separately to unblock it left 01a119e7 unable to apply ('this code link already exists'); it was replaced by these entries plus a status-only proposal. Lesson: with record trust, submit the committable changes in one call and the proposal-only ones (status, intent, rules) in another, so nothing committable waits on review.
